NoteQueen vs Rook Contiguity



Both methods define neighbours based on whether polygons share boundaries, but they use different rules.
Queen

Neighbour Definition: Share an edge or a vertex
Main Advantage: More inclusive and usually gives better connectivity Main
Main Limitation: Corner-touching areas may not have meaningful interaction

Rook

Neighbour Definition: Share an edge only
Main Advantage: Uses a stricter and more direct boundary relationship
Main Limitation: May exclude some nearby areas that only meet at a corner

How to Choose?

Use Queen contiguity when general spatial proximity and connectivity are important.
Use Rook contiguity when interaction is expected mainly through a shared boundary.
The choice should depend on the spatial process and research question, not on which method produces more neighbours.

To summarize, Queen is more inclusive, while Rook is more restrictive.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 - Technical Report
text:
This is Technical Report of Take-home Exercise 1, aiming to examine the spatial patterns of road traffic accidents in the Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area (BGMA) in 2022. Dataset from Kaggle Thailand Road Accident 2019-2022 is used. Administrative boundary data and road network data will also be incorporated to support spatial and network-constrained analyses.
The analysis consists of four main tasks:

Data Preparation and Quality Assessment: Clean and validate the accident records, define the study area, handle missing or invalid coordinates, and prepare the spatial datasets for analysis.
Exploratory and First-Order Analysis: Examine the spatial and temporal distribution of accidents and identify areas or road segments with high accident intensity using methods such as Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and Network Kernel Density Estimation (NKDE).
Second-Order Analysis – Investigate whether road accidents exhibit statistically significant spatial clustering, with particular attention to clustering along the road network.
Integration and Interpretation – Compare findings from conventional and network-constrained approaches and discuss their implications for road-safety planning and public-safety management.

NoteJoining Technics



A general way to joining data table is using by = join_by(), to identify which variable used for join.




Mapping GDPPC

basemap <- tm_shape(hunan) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_text("NAME_3", size=0.5)

  tm_layout(
    legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))
tmap_arrange(basemap, gdppc, asp=1, ncol=2)














NoteAbout qtm()



qtm() function has a default colour design as blue. Make sure to adjust the legend position, to not blocking the map.




Converting to Spatial Polygon Dataframe

hunan_sp <- hunan%>%
  as_Spatial()



Geographically Weighted Summary Statistics (GSWW) with adaptive bandwidth

bw_CV <- bw.gwr(GDPPC ~ 1,
                data = hunan_sp,
                approach = "CV",
                adaptive = TRUE,
                kernel = "bisquare",
                longlat = T)

NoteBandwidth selection for basic GWR



bw.gwr() is a function for automatic bandwidth selection to calibrate a basic GWR model.
Usage: bw.gwr(formula, data, approach=“CV”, kernel=“bisquare”, adaptive=FALSE, p=2, theta=0, longlat=F, dMat, parallel.method=F,parallel.arg=NULL) *CV here stands for Cross-Verification
CV vs AIC:

AICc: Select a bandwidth by balancing goodness-of-fit and model complexity. A lower AICc indicates a better trade-off and helps reduce overfitting.
Cross-Validation (CV): Select a bandwidth by minimising out-of-sample prediction error, commonly using leave-one-out prediction. A lower CV score indicates better predictive performance.

In summary

AICc


Focus on predictive performance

Computing geographically weighted summary statistics

gwstat <- gwss(data = hunan_sp,
               vars = "GDPPC",
               bw = bw_AIC,
               kernel = "bisquare",
               quantile = TRUE,
               adaptive = TRUE,
               longlat = T)



Preparing the output data

gwstat_df <- as.data.frame(gwstat$SDF)


hunan_gstat <- cbind(hunan, gwstat_df)

::: {.callout-note title: Why using cbind() here?} The reason cannot using leftjoin as previous is there is no unique identifier in gwstat_df dataset. Thus cbind() is used, by combining using same order. (Sequence never change)
Thus, if sorting is done, cannot use cbind() in this case, since sequence has been changed. :::


Visualising geographically weighted summary statistics

tm_shape(hunan_gstat) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "GDPPC_LM",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Local Mean")) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + 
  tm_title("Distribution of geographically weighted mean") + 
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))

title: Take-home Exercise 1 - Technical Report
text:
1.3 Event and Attribute Preparation

1.3.1 Define accident events
A point event represents one recorded road traffic accident occurring within the Bangkok Metropolitan Region during 2022. Each unique acc_code is treated as one event. Multiple accidents occurring at the same recorded coordinates are retained as separate events because they represent distinct accident incidents.


1.3.2 Derive Temporal Attributes

accident_bmr <- accident_bmr %>%
  mutate(
    month = month(incident_datetime, label = TRUE),
    weekday = wday(incident_datetime, label = TRUE),
    hour = hour(incident_datetime))



1.3.3 Derive Accident Severity

accident_bmr <- accident_bmr %>%
  mutate(
    severity = case_when(
      is.na(number_of_fatalities) | is.na(number_of_injuries) ~ "Unknown",
      number_of_fatalities > 0 ~ "Fatal",
      number_of_injuries > 0 ~ "Injury",
      TRUE ~ "Non-injury"))

::: Point-to-Network Validation Before conducting network-constrained spatial analysis, the distance from each accident point to its nearest road segment was calculated to assess positional consistency. The median distance was approximately 3.85 m, while 95% and 99% of accident locations were within approximately 10.58 m and 13.96 m of the nearest road, respectively. The maximum observed distance was approximately 41.53 m. These results suggest that the accident locations were generally well aligned with the road network. A maximum snapping tolerance of 50 m was therefore considered appropriate for projecting accident points onto the road network. :::
